paragraphs: Sequencing a genomic mixture produces many fragments drawn from different underlying sequences. Reconstructing haplotypes or viral strains therefore requires deciding which fragments came from the same source. Repeated coverage supplies useful evidence, but the grouping problem is computationally difficult and becomes more challenging as mixture components grow in number and length.

The paper proposes a convolutional auto-encoder that maps sequencing reads into a lower-dimensional representation. From these learned features, the method estimates the probability that each read belongs to a particular source. It then combines reads assigned to the same source into a consensus sequence. This connects representation learning directly to the grouping step needed for reconstruction.

Dimensionality reduction and mini-batch stochastic gradient descent help the method handle large collections of long reads. Experiments with simulated, semi-experimental, and experimental data show accurate reconstruction of haplotypes and viral mixtures, often outperforming existing methods. The findings support learned read representations as a practical way to improve reconstruction, without claiming that they remove the underlying computational difficulty.
neurips-2020-a-convolutional-auto-encode.tldr: A convolutional auto-encoder learns compact sequencing-read features that support accurate grouping and reconstruction of haplotypes and viral strains.

paragraphs: Neural tangent kernel analysis explains some neural-network training through a kernel function that describes how the network responds to parameter updates. Existing analyses rely on weights remaining very close to their starting values. They also cannot accommodate regularization or gradient noise, creating a gap between the theoretical picture and training procedures that include these ingredients.

This paper extends that analysis to noisy gradient descent with weight decay. Its central result is that training can still behave like a kernel method even with these modifications. The contribution is therefore an expanded theoretical account of optimization: adding noise and a penalty on weights need not eliminate the kernel-like behavior that makes training mathematically tractable.

The analysis implies linear convergence of training loss up to a specified accuracy level, rather than unrestricted convergence to zero. It also establishes a generalization-error bound for two-layer networks trained this way. Together, these results address both progress on the training objective and performance beyond the training data within the paper's analyzed setting.
neurips-2020-a-generalized-neural-tangen.tldr: A generalized neural tangent kernel analysis explains convergence and generalization for two-layer networks trained with gradient noise and weight decay.

paragraphs: Recommendation feedback depends on which items users had an opportunity to see. Consequently, observed responses reflect both preferences and exposure. The paper shows theoretically that supervised learning can produce inconsistent preference estimates when exposure information is absent. This matters for evaluation as well as training, because the observed feedback is shaped by the same selection mechanism.

Counterfactual propensity weighting tries to account for exposure, but partially observed feedback can leave the underlying quantities impossible to identify uniquely. The authors address this problem with a minimax empirical-risk formulation. This makes the uncertainty associated with exposure part of the learning problem instead of treating the observed feedback as a complete account of user preferences.

A relaxation of the formulation's dual becomes an adversarial game between two recommendation models. One is the candidate recommender; its opponent represents the exposure mechanism. The paper supplies learning bounds and extensive simulations across recommendation settings. These results support the proposed formulation as a principled approach to learning and evaluation when exposure complicates the interpretation of feedback.
neurips-2020-adversarial-counterfactual-.tldr: An adversarial minimax formulation addresses exposure-related uncertainty in recommendation learning and evaluation.

paragraphs: Discrete graphical models describe how many variables depend on one another. Learning those dependencies efficiently is difficult, and the abstract identifies maximum-likelihood reconstruction as intractable for the problem considered. The paper develops an approach based on Interaction Screening that aims to recover both the dependency structure and its numerical parameters using relatively little data.

The framework accommodates different sets of possible values at different nodes, interactions involving multiple variables, and arbitrary choices of basis for expressing those interactions. This breadth matters because it avoids restricting the analysis to a single narrowly specified model family. The recovery guarantees depend on one condition concerning model parameterization, which the authors say is readily checkable for a large class of models.

Under that condition, the analysis gives guarantees for structure and parameter recovery in any error norm. Its bounds distinguish properties of the underlying model from prior information supplied to the algorithm. The framework also contains previously studied models as special cases, and the analysis systematically improves their sample-complexity bounds.
neurips-2020-efficient-learning-of-discr.tldr: Interaction Screening supports sample-efficient recovery of general discrete graphical models under a verifiable parameterization condition.

paragraphs: Normalization and activation usually appear together in deep networks, yet they are commonly designed as separate components. This paper searches for them jointly. It represents a combined layer as a computation graph built from elementary operations such as addition, multiplication, and statistical moments, allowing the search to explore arrangements beyond established layer designs.

Searching at this low level creates a large space with relatively few useful candidates. The authors develop rejection procedures that quickly discard poor layers and use multi-objective evolution to assess performance across several architectures. Evaluating candidates across architectures is intended to prevent the search from producing a layer suited too narrowly to one network.

The resulting EvoNorm layers sometimes depart from familiar patterns: some do not center feature maps, require an explicit activation function, or separate normalization and activation into successive steps. Experiments show successful use in image classification and transfer to instance segmentation and image synthesis. EvoNorms outperform BatchNorm- and GroupNorm-based layers in many tested cases, supporting joint automated design as a productive alternative.
neurips-2020-evolving-normalization-acti.tldr: An evolutionary search jointly designs normalization and activation layers that perform well across several architectures and visual tasks.

paragraphs: Choosing a small, representative subset of a dataset can preserve useful information while avoiding excessive repetition. Submodular maximization is used for this kind of selection, but the resulting summary can underrepresent or overrepresent groups defined by sensitive attributes. The paper asks whether fairness constraints can be incorporated when datasets are large enough to require streaming methods.

The authors develop streaming approximation algorithms that optimize a submodular objective while respecting fairness constraints. Their methods cover both monotone and non-monotone objectives: settings where adding an item cannot reduce the objective, and settings where it can. This extends fairness-aware selection across two distinct kinds of summary-quality objectives rather than addressing only the simpler case.

The algorithms are evaluated on exemplar-based clustering, movie recommendation, DPP-based summarization, and maximum coverage in social networks. In these experiments, imposing fairness constraints does not significantly reduce utility. The result suggests that representative group inclusion and useful summaries can coexist in the tested applications, while the approximation algorithms provide a theoretical basis for handling the streaming setting.
neurips-2020-fairness-in-streaming-submo.tldr: Streaming approximation algorithms incorporate fairness constraints into submodular selection with little observed utility loss in the evaluated applications.

paragraphs: Robustness certification seeks mathematical assurance about a classifier's behavior when an adversary modifies its inputs. The paper studies nearest-prototype classifiers, including learning vector quantization and large-margin nearest neighbor, as a route to efficient certification. These models assign labels through comparisons with representative examples, making their distance-based structure central to the analysis.

The key quantity is the hypothesis margin, which measures separation relevant to changing a prediction. The authors prove that, when a classifier's dissimilarity comes from a seminorm, this margin gives a tight lower bound on adversarial attack size and can be calculated in constant time. The seminorm requirement is part of the result, linking the certificate to the classifier's chosen geometry.

The paper also shows that training these classifiers with a triplet loss maximizes the hypothesis margin, connecting the training objective directly to robustness. In the reported evaluation, classifiers optimized this way are competitive with state-of-the-art methods. Their certification complexity is a central advantage: the same structural analysis supports both robustness-oriented learning and fast guarantees.
neurips-2020-fast-adversarial-robustness.tldr: For nearest-prototype classifiers using seminorm-based dissimilarities, the hypothesis margin provides a tight, constant-time robustness certificate.

paragraphs: Understanding a three-dimensional point cloud requires information about the whole scene as well as local features. This paper adapts a contextual encoding layer from two-dimensional tasks to point clouds. The layer learns representative code words in feature space and uses them to construct a global descriptor that reweights the network's feature maps.

Point-cloud sparsity creates a difficulty: adding more code words quickly stops improving ordinary contextual encoding. The proposed solution divides feature channels into groups and encodes each group's feature vectors separately. This lets the model learn global context within smaller feature subspaces, addressing the observed saturation through a change in how features are organized.

Experiments across three point-cloud tasks show improvements over non-grouped encoding. Relative to VoteNet, the method gains 3 mAP on SUN-RGBD at the 0.25 threshold and 6.57 mAP on ScanNet at the 0.5 threshold. It also reaches 86% accuracy, a reported 1.5% improvement over PointNet++. These findings support grouped context encoding as useful across the evaluated settings.
neurips-2020-group-contextual-encoding-f.tldr: Encoding global point-cloud context in groups of feature channels improves results across the paper's evaluated 3D tasks.

paragraphs: A scientist may want to identify sets of features that provide overlapping information and determine which sets matter for classification. A single grouping for an entire dataset can miss an important possibility: both group membership and group relevance may change from one example to another. This paper makes that example-specific structure the object of learning.

The authors define two forms of redundancy through information theory, called representation redundancy and relevant redundancy. These definitions underpin a formulation for discovering feature groups separately for each instance. The theory also provides guidance on choosing an appropriate number of groups, connecting that design decision to the redundancy framework rather than leaving it entirely arbitrary.

To optimize the formulation, the method approximates mutual information with a variational lower bound and learns grouping and selection indicators using Gumbel-Softmax. Synthetic experiments validate the theoretical claims. Results on MNIST, Fashion MNIST, and gene-expression data show discovered groups alongside high classification accuracy, suggesting that identifying sample-dependent feature structure can remain compatible with useful prediction.
neurips-2020-instance-wise-feature-group.tldr: An information-theoretic method discovers redundant feature groups and their classification relevance separately for each example.

paragraphs: A classifier's confidence scores should provide useful information about the reliability of its predictions. Post-hoc calibration adjusts these scores after the original network has been trained. The challenge addressed here is to make that adjustment expressive enough for complex networks while preserving their predicted class rankings, including the classes appearing among their top-k choices.

The paper introduces intra order-preserving functions and a neural architecture that represents a class of them using common network components. Keeping the ordering intact allows confidence values to change without changing which classes the original model ranks highest. This supplies additional flexibility for calibration while maintaining the predictions responsible for the network's classification accuracy.

The authors also introduce order-invariant and diagonal subfamilies. These more restricted choices can regularize calibration and improve generalization when little training data is available. Evaluations span multiple datasets and classifiers, with the proposed method outperforming temperature scaling and Dirichlet calibration on several metrics. The findings support richer calibration functions whose structure explicitly protects prediction order.
neurips-2020-intra-order-preserving-func.tldr: Order-preserving neural calibration functions adjust confidence scores flexibly while retaining a classifier's top-k predictions.

paragraphs: Normalization layers are widely used because they often help deep networks train and generalize. Their success raises a separate question: whether good performance actually requires these layers. This paper investigates that question by studying networks with normalization removed and developing a method for training them without the performance degradation that removal might otherwise cause.

The contribution is a demonstrated alternative training approach for deep networks without normalization layers. Its significance lies in separating the benefits commonly associated with normalization from the claim that normalization itself is indispensable. Showing that another approach can achieve comparable results provides a way to reconsider the role these layers play in successful training.

The reported evaluations cover ImageNet classification, MS-COCO detection and segmentation, Kinetics video classification, and WMT English–German translation. Across a variety of tasks, the proposed method matches or slightly improves performance. These findings establish a competitive alternative in the tested settings and motivate further understanding of normalization; they do not establish that removing normalization will improve every network or task.
neurips-2020-is-normalization-indispensa.tldr: The paper demonstrates training deep networks without normalization layers while matching or slightly improving performance across several tasks.

paragraphs: In a latent bandit problem, an agent knows how actions generate rewards conditional on a hidden discrete state. Its online task is to identify that state so it can choose well. This connects offline model learning with online adaptation: a complex model can already be available, while interaction reveals which of its latent states applies.

The paper develops general algorithms based on upper confidence bounds and Thompson sampling. The algorithms incorporate context and account for uncertainty and misspecification in the model. This matters because the agent's decision problem involves both choosing actions and interpreting feedback through a model that may not be perfectly known or correctly specified.

A unified theoretical analysis shows lower regret than classic bandit policies when there are fewer latent states than actions. That condition captures the value of the hidden-state structure: learning which state applies can be more advantageous than treating the actions independently. An extensive empirical study further demonstrates advantages of the approach, with recommendation systems identified as a motivating application.
neurips-2020-latent-bandits-revisited-33.tldr: Contextual latent-bandit algorithms exploit hidden-state structure and achieve lower regret than classic policies when latent states are fewer than actions.

paragraphs: Sinkhorn divergences compare probability distributions using entropy-regularized optimal transport. Their computation typically involves a kernel matrix containing all pairwise relationships between support points. With n points, this creates a quadratic computational burden, and the matrix must be applied to vectors repeatedly during the iterative solution.

The paper replaces this full representation with positive feature vectors of dimension r, where r is much smaller than n. Kernel values become inner products between those vectors, with corresponding ground costs defined through a negative logarithm. This factorized structure reduces the cost of Sinkhorn iterations to O(nr), making the dependence on support size linear for fixed feature dimension.

The authors show that usual cost functions can be approximated in this form. The approximations also remain fully differentiable with respect to the input distributions, which is useful when distribution comparison forms part of a learning objective. They use that property to train a faster OT-GAN variant, connecting the computational construction to an application that needs gradients through optimal transport.
neurips-2020-linear-time-sinkhorn-diverg.tldr: Positive low-dimensional features reduce Sinkhorn iteration costs to O(nr) while retaining differentiability for learning applications.

paragraphs: Learning a linear dynamical system requires fitting observed behavior, but the resulting dynamics may also need to be stable. This paper develops an optimization method that combines these requirements. Using a characterization of stable matrices, the algorithm maintains stability at every step while iteratively improving reconstruction error through derived gradient directions.

For systems with external inputs, the method updates both the state matrix and the control matrix. Allowing both to change expands the set of candidate solutions compared with approaches that do not jointly update them. This creates opportunities to fit observations more accurately while preserving the stability requirement throughout optimization.

The paper evaluates the algorithm in simulations and experiments, including dynamic textures learned from image sequences and control of a robotic manipulator. It reports orders-of-magnitude improvements in reconstruction error and better control performance than existing approaches. The method also has a proven O(n²) memory requirement, compared with O(n⁴) for competing alternatives, enabling higher-dimensional systems in cases where those alternatives fail.
neurips-2020-memory-efficient-learning-o.tldr: A stability-preserving algorithm learns linear dynamical systems with improved reported fit and control performance using O(n²) memory.

paragraphs: The paper studies how difficult it is to learn halfspaces and ReLU functions when inputs follow a standard Gaussian distribution but labels can be arbitrary. This is an agnostic setting: the learner cannot assume that any function in the target class explains the labels perfectly. Instead, it aims to approach the best fit available within that class.

For halfspaces, success means a classification error at most epsilon above that of the best halfspace. For ReLUs, the corresponding target uses squared error. These definitions separate unavoidable error in the best-fitting function from the learner's additional error, making epsilon the required closeness to the best attainable fit.

The authors prove lower bounds of d raised to a polynomial in 1/epsilon in the Statistical Query model for both problems. Thus, the bounds express substantial difficulty as dimension and accuracy demands increase. They provide strong evidence that existing upper bounds are essentially optimal, while remaining bounds within the Statistical Query framework rather than unrestricted impossibility results for every learning algorithm.
neurips-2020-near-optimal-sq-lower-bound.tldr: Statistical Query lower bounds suggest existing algorithms for agnostic halfspace and ReLU learning under Gaussian inputs are essentially optimal.

paragraphs: Cooperating agents need to choose actions and decide whom to communicate with. This paper seeks communication structures that preserve effective joint planning while limiting each agent's communication burden. It measures that burden through the maximum degree of the communication graph, reflecting settings where agents have limited bandwidth.

Choosing a sparse graph is a combinatorial problem that the authors cannot solve directly through neural-network gradient descent. Their approach splits the task into two stages. First, they train a transformer policy that implicitly creates a soft communication graph. They then synthesize a programmatic policy that converts this soft structure into explicit communication choices.

The resulting neurosymbolic transformer combines a program that generates the communication graph with a transformer network that selects actions. This makes the communication structure an explicit part of the control policy. Experiments demonstrate low-degree communication graphs while maintaining near-optimal performance, supporting the two-stage approach as a way to reduce communication without sacrificing much coordination quality in the tested problems.
neurips-2020-neurosymbolic-transformers-.tldr: A learned transformer and synthesized communication program produce sparse multi-agent communication graphs with near-optimal experimental performance.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes one-hidden-layer networks with quadratic activations in an overparameterized setting where hidden-layer width exceeds input dimension. It uses a teacher–student setup: a teacher network generates the target relationship, and a student with the same architecture type and at least as much hidden width tries to recover it.

The authors examine how the number of training samples and the teacher's width shape the empirical loss landscape. In particular, they characterize how the probability of having no spurious minima depends on sample count, input dimension, and teacher width. This identifies conditions under which the optimization landscape permits recovery of the teacher rather than trapping learning at misleading minima.

Under the same conditions, the analysis shows that gradient descent converges and achieves small generalization error. This connects the possibility of recovery to a concrete learning procedure. The paper also characterizes convergence speed in the large-sample limit and confirms its results numerically. The conclusions concern the specified quadratic teacher–student setting, where optimization and generalization can be studied together.
neurips-2020-optimization-and-generaliza.tldr: For overparameterized quadratic teacher–student networks, the paper identifies conditions connecting favorable loss landscapes, gradient-descent convergence, and generalization.

paragraphs: Policy-gradient methods directly optimize a policy's performance and support rich policy representations, but their local updates can leave important parts of an environment unexplored. This paper addresses that weakness with PC-PG. Its central mechanism is a policy cover: an ensemble of learned policies used to guide the balance between exploration and exploitation.

The authors prove polynomial sample complexity and runtime for tabular Markov decision processes and for linear Markov decision processes in an infinite-dimensional reproducing kernel Hilbert space. These results give the exploration mechanism a formal efficiency guarantee within those settings, connecting policy-gradient learning to a provable way of gathering useful experience.

The analysis also considers misspecification. It provides state-aggregation guarantees under an average-case approximation-error assumption, plus guarantees under a broader assumption controlling approximation error when distributions shift. These conditions extend beyond standard worst-case uniform-error assumptions. Empirical evaluations span reward-free and reward-driven settings, complementing the theory with tests of the algorithm across different kinds of exploration tasks.
neurips-2020-pc-pg-policy-cover-directed.tldr: PC-PG uses an ensemble of policies to guide exploration, with efficiency and misspecification guarantees under the analyzed assumptions.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning policies often use randomness to support exploration, with entropy regularization encouraging stochastic behavior. In continuous action spaces, however, computing or incorporating entropy can become difficult for expressive policy architectures. The paper targets this obstacle: how to encourage useful randomness without requiring complex inference procedures tied to the policy's distribution.

The authors propose a regularizer compatible with a broad range of expressive policies. Its terms can be estimated simply and efficiently even when the policy distributions are unknown. This property matters because it lets the learning procedure encourage stochasticity without needing the same distributional access that makes conventional entropy regularization challenging in these settings.

Using the regularizer, the paper constructs an off-policy actor–critic algorithm and shows that the approach can promote exploration in continuous action spaces. Experiments report better performance than state-of-the-art regularized reinforcement-learning methods on continuous-control tasks. These findings support the regularizer as a practical component for expressive policies, with the reported gains applying to the tasks evaluated.
neurips-2020-promoting-stochasticity-for.tldr: An efficiently estimated regularizer promotes exploration with expressive continuous-action policies, including policies with unknown distributions.

paragraphs: Object detectors represent objects using formats such as boxes, centers, or corners. Different formats can support different strengths in classification and localization, but their features are difficult to combine because they do not share a uniform spatial organization. This paper introduces a module that brings these representations together inside an existing detector.

The bridging visual representations module uses an attention-based decoder similar to a Transformer decoder. The detector's main representation supplies queries, while other representations supply key instances that enrich the query features. Key sampling and shared location embeddings make the decoder more efficient. The complete system can be trained end to end while retaining the detector's primary representation.

Experiments add the module to RetinaNet, Faster R-CNN, FCOS, and ATSS, reporting improvements of about 1.5–3.0 AP. A strong detector with a strong backbone improves by about 2.0 AP to reach 52.7 AP on COCO test-dev. The resulting RelationNet++ demonstrates that attention can make complementary visual representations useful within several established detection frameworks.
neurips-2020-relationnet-bridging-visual.tldr: RelationNet++ uses an efficient attention decoder to combine complementary object representations and improve several established detectors.

paragraphs: Disentangled representations aim to separate the underlying factors that generate data, making learned features easier to interpret and use. The paper addresses the inconsistent performance of unsupervised disentanglement methods. It first applies population-based training to variational autoencoders and demonstrates improved training consistency in a supervised setting.

The authors then use Unsupervised Disentanglement Ranking as a heuristic for scoring models during population-based training. They observe that this procedure tends to reliably separate only some generative factors. The recursive rPU-VAE approach builds on that behavior: train to convergence, remove the learned factors from the dataset, and repeat to discover additional factors.

Each round can label subsets of the data with the factors it has learned. Those labels are subsequently used to train a single model that disentangles the full dataset. The paper reports substantial improvements in unsupervised disentanglement performance and robustness across multiple datasets and metrics. Its central contribution is turning consistent partial disentanglement into a staged process for learning a more complete representation.
neurips-2020-robust-disentanglement-of-a.tldr: rPU-VAE repeatedly learns subsets of generative factors and uses the resulting labels to train a more fully disentangled model.

paragraphs: Distributed neural-network training can spend substantial resources communicating gradients between workers. Compression reduces that traffic, but existing methods may scale poorly as gradients build up or as training uses larger batches. This paper proposes ScaleComp, a sparsified gradient-compression technique designed to retain communication savings as the distributed system grows.

The method exploits similarities in gradient distributions across learners to construct a commutative compressor that keeps communication cost constant with respect to worker count. It also applies a low-pass filter to local gradient accumulations to mitigate large-batch effects. Theoretical analysis supplies convergence guarantees and establishes compatibility with gradient all-reduce, connecting the compression scheme to distributed aggregation.

Experiments across image, language, and speech applications report low overhead and direct reductions in gradient traffic. The method achieves compression rates of 70–150 times and scales to 64–80 learners and batches ten times larger than normal training, without significant accuracy loss. These results support its intended role: making gradient compression useful at larger training scales rather than only in smaller configurations.
neurips-2020-scalecom-scalable-sparsifie.tldr: ScaleComp combines commutative gradient compression with filtered accumulation to reduce communication while scaling distributed training.

paragraphs: Feature-attribution methods explain a network by assigning importance to parts of an input. Attacks can make those explanations differ sharply between nearby inputs, undermining their reliability. This paper studies that vulnerability through the geometry of the model, focusing on how rapidly its gradients change as inputs move.

The authors identify Lipschitz continuity conditions on model gradients that lead to robust gradient-based attributions. These conditions place bounds on gradient variation, linking smoother behavior to more stable explanations. They also observe that smoothness may help explain whether an attack transfers between attribution methods; that connection is presented as a possibility rather than a universal conclusion.

The paper proposes two mitigations: an inexpensive training regularizer that promotes the identified conditions, and stochastic smoothing that can be used without retraining. Experiments on multiple image models show that both consistently improve attribution robustness. The results connect a geometric explanation of the attacks with practical ways to reduce their effects on real, large-scale networks.
neurips-2020-smoothed-geometry-for-robus.tldr: Gradient-smoothness conditions motivate training regularization and retraining-free smoothing that improve attribution robustness in image-model experiments.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks trained on low-dimensional tasks are used to study biological network function, but it is less clear how training changes their connections. This paper examines networks trained by gradient descent on neuroscience-inspired tasks, asking how task structure and the network's initial random connectivity jointly shape learning.

The authors find that changes to recurrent connectivity can be described by low-rank matrices. This remains true when the initial connectivity is random and full rank. The distinction matters: learning can add a relatively low-dimensional modification to a much richer starting network. In the experiments, that random starting connectivity also substantially speeds training.

To explain these observations, the paper analyzes a simpler task with a linear recurrent network. This tractable setting shows how low-dimensional task structure produces low-rank connectivity changes and how random initial connections facilitate learning. Together, the empirical and analytical results suggest that structured changes and random initialization can work cooperatively, offering a perspective on learning that focuses on modifications to connectivity rather than only the final network.
neurips-2020-the-interplay-between-rando.tldr: RNNs trained on low-dimensional tasks develop low-rank connectivity changes, while full-rank random initialization can accelerate learning.

paragraphs: Variational inference learns an approximation to a posterior distribution by optimizing an objective such as the evidence lower bound, or ELBO. Noisy gradient estimates can make that optimization difficult. This paper analyzes an unbiased estimator based on the score-function method with leave-one-out control variates, which are used to reduce estimation noise.

The authors connect the estimator to a new objective called the log-variance loss. This loss measures the variance of the log-ratio between the exact posterior and its approximation. Under certain conditions, its gradient equals the gradient of the negative ELBO. That connection gives the estimator, named VarGrad, another interpretation grounded in variation of the posterior-to-approximation ratio.

The theoretical analysis establishes lower variance than the score-function method in certain settings and shows that the leave-one-out control-variate coefficients are close to optimal. Experiments on a discrete variational autoencoder find a favorable trade-off between variance and computation compared with other leading estimators. The findings support VarGrad's efficiency while preserving the conditions attached to its theoretical advantages.
neurips-2020-vargrad-a-low-variance-grad.tldr: VarGrad links an unbiased variational-inference gradient estimator to a log-variance objective and offers conditional variance reductions with favorable empirical efficiency.
